individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces TabINR, an auto-decoder-based implicit neural representation (INR) framework for tabular data imputation. The model maps row and feature embeddings to cell values via a shared MLP with SIREN activations, trained on observed entries with a mixed MSE/BCE loss. At inference, new rows are handled by optimizing a fresh row embedding while freezing the network and feature embeddings. Experiments on 12 UCI datasets under MCAR, MAR, and MNAR mechanisms at 10–70% missingness compare against mean/mode, KNN, MICE, MissForest, GAIN, and ReMasker, reporting NRMSE/AUROC and downstream XGBoost classification. The paper also includes permutation robustness and ablation studies.
Strengths: The proposed method is conceptually simple and unifies row/feature embeddings with auto-decoder-style test-time adaptation, which is a natural fit for tabular data and enables instance-specific imputation without retraining.

The evaluation covers a broad set of 12 datasets, three missingness mechanisms, and multiple missingness ratios, and the method is shown to be competitive or superior, especially on high-dimensional datasets.
The permutation robustness analysis is a thoughtful check that addresses a key concern about applying INRs to unordered tabular data.
Ablation studies over architecture dimensions and activations provide useful insights into model sensitivity and capacity trade-offs.
Weaknesses: Despite mentioning transformer-based methods (TabTransformer, FT-Transformer, SAINT) and VAE methods (MIWAE, HI-VAE) in related work, the experimental comparison includes only GAIN and ReMasker among deep generative baselines, limiting evidence for the claimed advantages.

The evaluation reporting is incomplete: results are only shown as aggregate figures in the appendix with no per-dataset numerical tables or significance tests, making it hard to verify claims and compare methods statistically.

The downstream classification setup is questionable: 'full-column imputation of the target variable' is an unusual protocol, and imputing the target before training a classifier can bias evaluation; standard practice would train on observed targets.

The training procedure includes random masking of 10–70% of entries in addition to the synthetically missing data, but the purpose and interaction with the missingness simulation are not clearly explained.

Test-time latent optimization cost is not analyzed in detail; the reported inference time appears to exclude the iterative optimization required for each new row, which could be substantial for large inference sets.

Details of categorical imputation and evaluation are vague: AUROC computation for multi-class one-hot features and the winner-takes-all projection are not fully specified, and MAR/MNAR synthesis is only briefly described.
Questions: How is AUROC computed for categorical features with multiple categories—per one-hot column, macro-averaged, or micro-averaged?
What exactly is 'full-column imputation of the target variable' in the downstream experiment, and why is this protocol preferred over training XGBoost on observed target values?
What is the role of random masking (10–70%) during training when missingness is already simulated? Is it applied per epoch and does it overlap with the evaluation mask?
How many gradient steps are used for test-time latent optimization, and how does the total inference time (including optimization for all new rows) compare with the reported forward-pass times?
Are the performance differences between TabINR and baselines statistically significant given the reported standard deviations and overlapping error bars?
Why were MIWAE and HI-VAE, as well as transformer-based imputers (SAINT, FT-Transformer), excluded from the empirical comparison despite being discussed in related work?
Limitations: The evaluation is limited to moderate-scale UCI datasets with synthetic missingness; real-world missing patterns and larger datasets are not explored.
The method uses a single global hyperparameter configuration across datasets, which may understate its best-case performance and limit generalizability claims.
MNAR imputation is fundamentally difficult, and TabINR does not explicitly model the missingness mechanism; its competitive MNAR results may not hold in more complex real-world settings.
No code or implementation details are provided, which hampers reproducibility.

Potential negative societal impacts include the risk that biased or inaccurate imputations in sensitive domains (e.g., healthcare, finance) could propagate biases into downstream decisions, though no specific new risks are identified.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces TabINR, an implicit neural representation (INR) framework for tabular data imputation. It models each table entry as a function of learnable row and feature embeddings through a shared MLP with SIREN activations, trained with a mixed MSE/BCE loss on observed entries. At inference, new rows can be adapted by optimizing only the row embedding while keeping the network and feature embeddings frozen. The authors evaluate on 12 UCI datasets under MCAR, MAR, and MNAR missingness at ratios 0.1-0.7, comparing with mean/mode, KNN, MICE, MissForest, GAIN, and ReMasker, reporting NRMSE/AUROC, inference time, permutation robustness, downstream classification, and ablations.
Strengths: The idea of modeling tables as implicit neural functions with learnable row and feature embeddings is a sensible and timely application of INRs to tabular imputation, and the test-time latent optimization provides instance-adaptive imputations.
The benchmark is broad: 12 datasets, three missingness mechanisms, multiple missingness ratios, and comparisons against classical and deep baselines, plus a downstream classification evaluation.
The permutation invariance experiment convincingly addresses a key concern about using coordinate-based INRs on data without natural ordering.
The inference-time comparison shows TabINR is faster than iterative imputers such as MICE and MissForest, which is practically relevant.
Weaknesses: The main imputation results are only described qualitatively ('consistently ranks among top', 'mostly matching or outperforming'); no per-dataset numerical tables with NRMSE/AUROC and standard deviations are provided in the text, making it impossible to verify the claims or perform statistical comparisons.
Several important baselines discussed in related work (MIWAE, HI-VAE, SAINT, FT-Transformer) are not included in experiments; the comparison set is limited to GAIN and ReMasker among deep methods.

The training protocol is ambiguous: Section 2.2 mentions random masking of 10–70% during training, while experiments use synthetically missing entries at a given ratio; it is unclear how these interact and how held-out entries are defined.

The MNAR mechanism is vaguely described as 'additionally applying Bernoulli masking to values left unmasked' without specifying how the masking probability depends on the values; without this, the mechanism cannot be reproduced and may not properly represent MNAR.
The categorical AUROC evaluation after one-hot expansion and winner-takes-all projection is not detailed; the metric could be inflated or misleading depending on how multiclass AUROC is aggregated.

The ablation study defines a separate default configuration (depth=4, latent=64) that differs from the global defaults (depth=2, latent=32), making the sensitivity analysis and the choice of global defaults difficult to interpret.
The claimed scalability advantages are mostly supported by sensitivity experiments on a single dataset (letter); broader evidence across datasets with varying sizes and dimensionality is missing.
Questions: What exactly is the training masking procedure? During training, do you additionally randomly mask observed entries to create a reconstruction objective, and how does that interact with the synthetic missingness ratio?

For the imputation benchmark, are row embeddings trained on rows with observed entries and missing entries imputed directly by forward pass, or is test-time latent optimization used for every row? How are new rows evaluated?
How is AUROC computed for categorical features with one-hot encoding? Is it micro/macro averaged per original categorical feature across all categories?

In the MNAR synthetic mechanism, what is the exact probability model for Bernoulli masking applied to values left unmasked? Does the masking probability depend on the value itself, and what parameters are used?
Why are MIWAE/HI-VAE/SAINT/FT-Transformer not included in experiments despite being discussed in related work? What are the computational constraints?
Can you provide per-dataset numerical results (tables) for all missingness mechanisms and ratios, with standard deviations, so claims can be assessed?
How does test-time adaptation perform when a new row has very few observed features (e.g., 10%)? Are there failure cases or instability?
Limitations: Evaluation is limited to synthetically generated missingness on UCI benchmarks; real-world missing data mechanisms may involve more complex dependencies.
The method is not evaluated on very large or very high-dimensional datasets, so claims about scalability beyond the tested range are unsupported.
A single global hyperparameter configuration is used; per-dataset tuning could yield different conclusions.
The test-time latent optimization requires observed features for each new row; performance for extremely sparse new rows (e.g., fewer than 10% observed features) is not analyzed.
Potential negative societal impact if used in high-stakes domains without careful validation of imputation quality; no specific harms identified.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper introduces TabINR, an implicit neural representation (INR) framework for tabular data imputation. It models each table cell as a function of learnable row and feature embeddings through an MLP, and uses an auto-decoder-style test-time latent optimization to adapt to unseen rows. The method is evaluated on 12 UCI datasets under MCAR, MAR, and MNAR missingness at rates from 10% to 70%, comparing against KNN, MICE, MissForest, GAIN, and ReMasker. The authors report competitive or superior imputation accuracy, especially on high-dimensional datasets, and additionally evaluate downstream classification, inference time, permutation robustness, and ablations.
Strengths: The proposed approach is conceptually simple and offers a different perspective from GAN/transformer-based imputers by casting tabular imputation as learning a neural function over row and feature embeddings.
The paper includes a broad experimental protocol: 12 datasets, three missingness mechanisms, multiple missingness ratios, downstream classification, runtime comparison, and permutation robustness.
Test-time latent optimization is a principled mechanism that allows the model to adapt to unseen instances without retraining the whole network.
Weaknesses: The main quantitative evidence is missing from the manuscript: no per-dataset NRMSE/AUROC tables are provided, and all result figures are redacted in the submitted version, making it impossible to verify the central claims.

The novelty is incremental: combining learnable row/column embeddings with an MLP closely resembles neural matrix factorization / collaborative filtering, and the auto-decoder idea is borrowed from DeepSDF; the paper does not adequately differentiate from these existing ideas.

The claim of fast inference contradicts the need to run gradient-based optimization for every new row; no details are given on the number of optimization steps, learning rate, initialization, or stopping criterion for this test-time procedure.

The description of the MNAR mechanism is questionable: adding Bernoulli masking to values left unmasked by a MAR mechanism does not clearly create missingness that depends on the missing values themselves.
The paper states that random masking of 10–70% is applied during training, but it is unclear how this interacts with the benchmark missingness mask; this could distort the evaluation setting.
Memory cost scales with the number of rows because each row has its own embedding, which conflicts with the 'memory-efficient' claim and is not analyzed or compared empirically.
Several relevant baselines mentioned in related work (MIWAE, HI-VAE, HyperImpute, FT-Transformer, SAINT) are not included in the experiments.

No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported; the standard deviations in the figures are not available in the text, and the downstream classification results lack specification of the missingness mechanism used.
Reproducibility is limited because no code is provided and many experimental details are omitted, such as the exact test-time optimization protocol and per-dataset hyperparameters.
Questions: How many gradient steps and what learning rate are used for the test-time latent optimization? Is convergence monitored, and how sensitive are results to these choices?
How is the benchmark missingness mask used during training given the additional random masking of 10–70%? Does the random masking replace the benchmark mask or is it applied on top?
Can the authors provide per-dataset NRMSE and AUROC tables with standard deviations across seeds, rather than only aggregated figures?
Does the reported inference time include the time for optimizing a new row embedding? If so, how is sub-0.25s achieved on datasets like letter?
What is the exact MNAR generation procedure? How does adding Bernoulli masking to values left unmasked create dependence on unobserved values?
How does memory consumption of TabINR scale with dataset size, and how does it compare to ReMasker in terms of parameters and memory?
Why are MIWAE, HI-VAE, HyperImpute, FT-Transformer, and SAINT omitted from the benchmark despite being discussed in related work?

In the downstream classification experiments, is the target column included in the missingness simulation, and what missingness mechanism is used? How is the 'Direct TabINR classifier' trained and evaluated?
Limitations: Evaluation is limited to synthetically induced missingness on moderate-scale UCI datasets; real-world missing data and complex missingness patterns are not explored.
A single global hyperparameter configuration is used, which the authors acknowledge likely underestimates the model's best-case performance.
The latest transformer-based imputers are not benchmarked, limiting the strength of the comparison.
The memory footprint and test-time optimization cost of per-row embeddings are not analyzed, raising questions about scalability to large datasets.
No theoretical analysis of the latent optimization's convergence or identifiability is provided.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces TabINR, an implicit neural representation (INR) framework for tabular data imputation. It models a table as a neural function mapping learnable row and feature embeddings to cell values, and employs an auto-decoder-style test-time latent optimization to impute unseen rows. The method is evaluated on twelve UCI datasets under MCAR, MAR, and MNAR missingness mechanisms with missing ratios from 0.1 to 0.7, comparing against classical (KNN, MICE, MissForest) and deep learning (GAIN, ReMasker) baselines. Results show competitive accuracy, especially on higher-dimensional datasets, and additional experiments cover inference time, permutation robustness, downstream classification, and ablations.
Strengths: Simple and unified framework: a single architecture handles mixed numerical and categorical features by combining row/feature embeddings with an MLP, making the approach conceptually clean.
Test-time adaptation via latent optimization allows imputation for unseen rows without retraining the network, which is a practical advantage.
Broad empirical evaluation across 12 datasets, three missingness mechanisms, and multiple missingness ratios, with competitive or superior performance on several benchmarks.
Permutation robustness is explicitly verified, which addresses a natural concern for INR applications to tabular data.
The paper includes downstream classification experiments, showing that imputations can be useful for subsequent predictive models.
Weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the method is a direct application of auto-decoder INRs (e.g., DeepSDF) to tabular data by introducing row/feature embeddings, which is a straightforward extension of existing ideas.

The claimed inference-time efficiency is misleading: test-time adaptation for a new row requires optimizing a fresh embedding, not just a forward pass, and the paper does not report the number of optimization steps or wall-clock time for this process.

Memory scaling is a concern: learning a row embedding for every training instance makes the parameter count grow linearly with dataset size, undermining the claimed memory-efficiency for large tabular datasets.
Evaluation lacks statistical significance testing, and differences between methods are often within one standard deviation; it is unclear which improvements are meaningful.

The benchmark omits several relevant deep imputation baselines (e.g., MIWAE, HI-VAE, SAINT) and only considers datasets with at most 57 features, which weakens the claim of advantages on high-dimensional data.

Experimental details are underspecified: AUROC computation for multi-class one-hot categoricals, MNAR generation specifics, number of seeds, and per-method hyperparameter choices are not fully described, hindering reproducibility.
The ablation study uses a different default configuration than the main experiments, making it hard to interpret how sensitive the results are to hyperparameter choices.
The winner-takes-all projection for categorical imputation ignores uncertainty and may produce imputations that are not representative of the underlying distribution.
Questions: How many gradient steps are used for test-time latent optimization, and what is the total wall-clock time to impute a new row? Does this remain within the reported sub-0.25s inference time?
How is AUROC computed for categorical features with more than two classes after one-hot expansion? Is it macro-averaged, micro-averaged, or per-binary-column?
How are the MAR and MNAR masks generated exactly, and are the same masks used for all methods?
What is the variance across random seeds, and are the reported differences statistically significant (e.g., via paired tests)?
Does the model need to be retrained for each missingness ratio, or is a single trained model used to impute at different missing rates?
How does the method scale to larger datasets (e.g., millions of rows) given the memory cost of per-row embeddings?
Limitations: Experiments are limited to synthetically induced missingness on fully observed UCI datasets; performance on real-world missing data with complex patterns is untested.
Dataset scale is modest (up to 20,000 rows and 57 features), so claims about scalability to high-dimensional or large-scale tabular data are not substantiated.
The test-time optimization cost is not properly accounted for in the efficiency comparison, potentially overstating the inference speed advantage.
Categorical imputation uses a winner-takes-all heuristic that may ignore prediction uncertainty and produce low-quality imputations for ambiguous cases.
No analysis of potential bias or fairness implications in downstream applications such as healthcare or finance is provided.

review.Summary: The paper introduces TabINR, an implicit neural representation (INR) framework for tabular data imputation. Tables are modeled as neural functions mapping learnable row and feature embeddings to cell values. Training uses only observed cells with a mixed MSE/BCE loss, and unseen rows are handled via auto-decoder-style test-time latent optimization. The authors benchmark TabINR on twelve UCI datasets under MCAR/MAR/MNAR missingness at rates 0.1–0.7, comparing against KNN, MICE, MissForest, GAIN, and ReMasker, and also evaluate downstream classification and inference time. They report competitive or superior accuracy, especially on high-dimensional data, and include ablation and permutation robustness studies.
Strengths: The formulation is simple and elegant: using row/feature embeddings with a shared MLP avoids hand-crafted imputation rules and naturally handles mixed continuous/categorical features.
Test-time latent optimization is a principled way to adapt to new rows without retraining the network, aligning with auto-decoder ideas from DeepSDF.
The experimental scope is broad: 12 datasets, three missingness mechanisms, four missingness ratios, downstream classification, runtime comparisons, and a permutation-robustness check.
The paper is generally clearly written and includes an honest limitations section, acknowledging synthetic missingness, fixed hyperparameters, and missing transformer baselines.
Weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not verifiable from the submitted text: all detailed benchmark results are in redacted figures (Figures 3, 6–27), and no numerical NRMSE/AUROC tables for the full dataset set are provided. Only a single ablation table (letter) and a downstream table (5 datasets) are shown.

The synthetic MNAR mechanism appears incorrectly implemented: the paper says MNAR 'extends MAR by additionally applying Bernoulli masking to values left unmasked,' which adds MCAR-like missingness after MAR and does not make missingness depend on the missing values themselves. Thus the MNAR results may not reflect true MNAR settings.

The model requires a learnable embedding per training row, so memory grows linearly with dataset size. The claim of being 'memory-efficient' is not supported, especially since experiments only use datasets up to 20k rows.

The benchmark omits several relevant deep imputation baselines, including MIWAE, HI-VAE, SAINT, TabTransformer, and FT-Transformer, despite these being discussed in related work. Only ReMasker represents modern deep models.

Inference-time adaptation still requires an iterative optimization loop for each new row; details such as number of gradient steps, initialization sensitivity, and behavior under very sparse observations are not provided.

No statistical significance tests are reported; the 'winning' claims are based on mean/std in a limited set of datasets and missingness settings, and differences are often within one standard deviation.
Questions: Can the authors include full numerical result tables for all 12 datasets, all missingness mechanisms, and all rates, instead of only redacted figures?

How exactly is the MNAR missingness generated? Is the additional Bernoulli masking applied independently of the values, and if so, how does this create dependence of missingness on the unobserved values?
How many optimization iterations are used for test-time row embedding inference, and how does performance vary with the number of observed features per row?
How does the memory footprint of storing one row embedding per training row compare with baselines on datasets with millions of rows?
Why were MIWAE, HI-VAE, TabTransformer, and FT-Transformer not included in the empirical comparison despite being discussed as relevant prior work?
How robust is the test-time latent optimization to local minima or poor initialization, especially when only one or two features are observed?
Limitations: The evaluation is limited to moderate-sized UCI datasets with synthetically induced missingness; real-world missing data patterns and domain knowledge are not explored.
The claimed MNAR experiments are likely invalid because the generated missingness mechanism does not correctly simulate missing-not-at-random data.
A single global hyperparameter configuration is used across all datasets, which may understate TabINR's best-case performance and makes it unclear how much tuning is needed for new datasets.
Categorical imputation uses a winner-takes-all projection, which discards uncertainty and may produce biased or overconfident predictions for high-cardinality categories.
No discussion of negative societal impacts is provided; in high-stakes applications, imputation errors or biased imputations could propagate into downstream decisions.

review.Summary: The paper introduces TabINR, an auto-decoder-based implicit neural representation (INR) framework for tabular data imputation. It models each table entry as a function of learnable row and feature embeddings through a shared MLP with SIREN activations, trained on observed entries with a mixed MSE/BCE loss. At inference, new rows are handled by optimizing a fresh row embedding while freezing the network and feature embeddings. The method is evaluated on 12 UCI datasets under MCAR, MAR, and MNAR missingness at ratios 10–70%, comparing against mean/mode, KNN, MICE, MissForest, GAIN, and ReMasker, reporting NRMSE/AUROC, downstream XGBoost classification, inference time, permutation robustness, and ablations.
Strengths: Conceptually simple and unified framework using row/feature embeddings with an MLP and SIREN activations, naturally handling mixed continuous/categorical features.
Broad experimental protocol covering 12 datasets, three missingness mechanisms, multiple missingness ratios, downstream classification, runtime comparison, and permutation robustness.
Test-time latent optimization provides a principled way to adapt to unseen rows without retraining the network, which is a practical advantage.
Permutation robustness is explicitly verified, addressing a key concern about applying coordinate-based INRs to unordered tabular data.
Inference-time comparison shows TabINR is faster than iterative imputers such as MICE and MissForest, which is practically relevant.
Weaknesses: The main quantitative results are not verifiable from the submitted text: only aggregate or redacted figures are provided, with no per-dataset numerical NRMSE/AUROC tables or statistical significance tests.

Several relevant deep imputation baselines discussed in related work (MIWAE, HI-VAE, SAINT, FT-Transformer, TabTransformer, HyperImpute) are omitted from the empirical comparison, limiting the strength of the claims.

The reported inference time likely excludes the iterative gradient-based optimization required for each new row's embedding; details on the number of steps, learning rate, initialization, and stopping criterion are missing.
Memory cost scales linearly with the number of rows due to storing a row embedding per training instance, conflicting with the 'memory-efficient' claim and not analyzed or compared empirically.

The synthetic MNAR mechanism is likely invalid: adding Bernoulli masking to values left unmasked after MAR does not create missingness that depends on the missing values themselves, so the MNAR results may not reflect true MNAR settings.

The training protocol is ambiguous: additional random masking of 10–70% of entries during training is mentioned, but its interaction with the benchmark missingness mask and the held-out evaluation mask is not clearly explained.

Categorical imputation evaluation is underspecified: AUROC computation for multi-class one-hot features and the winner-takes-all projection are not fully detailed, and the latter discards uncertainty and may produce biased imputations.

The ablation study uses a different default configuration (depth=4, latent=64) than the main experiments (depth=2, latent=32), making the sensitivity analysis and the choice of global defaults difficult to interpret.

Novelty is incremental: combining learnable row/column embeddings with an MLP closely resembles neural matrix factorization or collaborative filtering, and the auto-decoder concept is borrowed from DeepSDF without sufficient differentiation.
No code or implementation details are provided, and many experimental details (e.g., number of seeds, per-dataset hyperparameters, exact MNAR generation) are omitted, hindering reproducibility.
A single global hyperparameter configuration is used across all datasets, which the authors acknowledge likely underestimates the model's best-case performance and limits generalizability claims.
Questions: How many gradient steps and what learning rate are used for test-time latent optimization, and does the reported inference time include this optimization?
What is the exact MNAR generation procedure? How does adding Bernoulli masking to values left unmasked create missingness dependent on the missing values themselves?
Can the authors provide per-dataset numerical NRMSE and AUROC tables with standard deviations and statistical significance tests (e.g., paired tests) for all datasets and missingness settings?
Why are MIWAE, HI-VAE, SAINT, FT-Transformer, and TabTransformer omitted from the empirical benchmark despite being discussed as relevant prior work?
How is AUROC computed for categorical features with more than two classes after one-hot expansion? Is it macro-averaged, micro-averaged, or per-binary-column?
How does the memory footprint of TabINR scale with dataset size, and how does it compare with baselines on large or high-dimensional datasets?
What is the role of the additional random masking (10–70%) during training, and how does it interact with the synthetic missingness masks used for evaluation?
How robust is test-time latent optimization when a new row has very few observed features (e.g., 10%)? Are there failure cases or instability, and how is it initialized?
Limitations: Evaluation is limited to moderate-scale UCI datasets (up to ~20,000 rows and 57 features) with synthetically induced missingness; real-world missing data patterns and larger datasets are not explored.
The MNAR experiments are likely invalid because the generated missingness mechanism does not correctly simulate missing-not-at-random data.
Memory and test-time optimization costs are not properly analyzed, raising concerns about scalability to very large datasets and to sparse new rows.
A single global hyperparameter configuration is used, which may understate TabINR's best-case performance and makes it unclear how much tuning is needed for new datasets.
Categorical imputation uses a winner-takes-all projection that ignores prediction uncertainty and may produce biased or overconfident predictions for high-cardinality categories.
No code or implementation details are provided, limiting reproducibility.

Potential negative societal impacts include the risk that biased or inaccurate imputations in sensitive domains (e.g., healthcare, finance) could propagate into downstream decisions, though no specific new risks are identified.
